findings.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/AuthzClient.java:95 — P1, confidence 100: `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader());` couples ordinary client construction to a process-global first-write-wins singleton, so when an isolated authz classloader initializes first with only the new order-100 provider, a later initialization from a classloader containing the default or FIPS provider is skipped and every common crypto consumer remains bound to the mostly unsupported stand-in; the strongest counterargument is that order-200 providers win when co-visible, but priority is never reconsidered after the first initialization and therefore cannot repair cross-classloader or initialization-order pinning.

common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — P1, confidence 100: `.sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed())` followed by `return foundProviders.get(0);` changes the multiple-provider invariant from fail-fast to arbitrary winner selection, so when any two full providers are visible their identical `return 200;` priorities tie and `ServiceLoader` encounter order silently chooses the process-wide implementation; the strongest counterargument is that ordering is required to let the authz fallback coexist, but rejecting a tie at the highest priority preserves that coexistence while retaining deterministic selection among mutually incompatible full providers.

common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoProvider.java:44 — P1, confidence 100: the new abstract SPI method `int order();` breaks every external `CryptoProvider` implementer compiled against the previous interface, because discovery now invokes the absent method through the comparator and terminates initialization with `AbstractMethodError`; the strongest counterargument is that every provider needs an explicit precedence, but a default method can assign legacy implementations a stable precedence without breaking the service-provider contract.

authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:75 — P2, confidence 100: the verbatim implementation `throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported yet.");` is repeated across 17 capabilities of a process-global `CryptoProvider`, so any current or future shared consumer outside the two ECDSA conversions receives a provider that violates its advertised abstraction; the strongest counterargument is that authz currently needs only ECDSA conversion, but that proves a narrow ECDSA fallback is the correct shape, and deleting the global provider registration in favor of that fallback makes the priority API, service metadata, and all 17 unsupported stand-in methods unnecessary.

authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:63 — P2, confidence 100: `return KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider();` implements `getBouncyCastleProvider()` by returning the JVM's default keystore provider rather than a Bouncy Castle provider, so once the authz stand-in is selected any consumer that uses this contract to obtain Bouncy Castle receives an unrelated implementation and propagates incorrect provider semantics; the strongest counterargument is that authz does not call this method today, but registering the object globally exposes the method to all consumers and a stand-in cannot safely satisfy an interface by changing the meaning of its methods.

authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:114 — P3, confidence 100: the two statements `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` allocate and populate throwaway encoders before the same values are encoded again into the returned sequence, adding four short-lived objects to every conversion with no state or validation effect; the strongest counterargument is that the calls document or pre-validate the integers, but `write(BigInteger)` cannot reject these already materialized values and the immediately repeated sequence writes perform the identical operation, so deleting both statements makes the throwaway encoders and their backing buffers unnecessary.

common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — P1, confidence 100: the selection rule `sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed())` is incomplete for ties because `DefaultCryptoProvider.order()`, `WildFlyElytronProvider.order()`, and `FIPS1402Provider.order()` all return `200` (crypto/default/src/main/java/org/keycloak/crypto/def/DefaultCryptoProvider.java:84, crypto/elytron/src/main/java/org/keycloak/crypto/elytron/WildFlyElytronProvider.java:77, crypto/fips1402/src/main/java/org/keycloak/crypto/fips/FIPS1402Provider.java:115); when any two production providers are present, the comparator cannot express a preference and line 71 silently selects whichever ServiceLoader enumerates first, so a FIPS deployment can select the non-FIPS provider instead of rejecting the ambiguous configuration.

common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoProvider.java:44 — P1, confidence 75: the new abstract contract `int order();` was added without a default implementation; when an existing ServiceLoader-discovered custom `CryptoProvider` compiled against the prior interface is carried across the upgrade, `CryptoProvider::order` invokes a missing method and startup fails with `AbstractMethodError`, so the change does not cover backward compatibility for the provider population it now enumerates.

authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:42 — P2, confidence 100: `keyPair = KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair();` creates one unparameterized provider-default curve and reuses it for ES256, ES384, and ES512; a single key cannot exercise the required P-256, P-384, and P-521 component widths, so at least two algorithm cases omit their real curve boundary and leave the corresponding ASN.1 length/padding behavior unverified.

authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:47 — P1, confidence 100: `AuthzClientCryptoProvider prov = new AuthzClientCryptoProvider();` bypasses both the service descriptor and `CryptoIntegration.init`, and the only assertion at line 56 is a private decoder→encoder→decoder round trip; when the packaged client starts with a missing/misread service entry, wrong provider priority, or DER bytes that only the matching custom decoder accepts, this test still passes, so the feature's actual AuthzClient discovery and signed-JWT interoperability acceptance criteria are not verified.

docs/metareview/reviews/mrv-20260911-004242054671000-task-done-task-001-6af4dd3d.md:40 — P1, confidence 100: the verbatim command `metareview fsm --workflow review-loop --base <ref>` omits the required `init` subcommand, so replacing `<ref>` and executing it triggers `ERR_USAGE: unknown subcommand --workflow` before any review workflow is created and cannot record the evidence required to clear the sole blocker.

common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoProvider.java:44 — P1, confidence 100: `int order();` works today, breaks when a deployment upgrades this interface while retaining a ServiceLoader provider compiled against the previous SPI: the comparator invokes the absent method and throws `AbstractMethodError` during `CryptoIntegration.init`, so crypto initialization and the calling application fail before any provider is selected; the strongest rebuttal is that providers can be recompiled for the release, but ServiceLoader is an external extension boundary and a default `order()` is required to preserve runtime compatibility with already-compiled implementations.

common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — P1, confidence 100: `.sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed())` followed by `return foundProviders.get(0);` works today, breaks when two highest-ranked providers coexist: all three production providers return `200`, so the stable sort preserves unspecified ServiceLoader encounter order and silently pins the process to an arbitrary implementation, producing environment-dependent crypto behavior instead of the prior deterministic startup failure; the strongest rebuttal is that normal packaging includes only one production provider, but accidental transitive overlap and container classloader enumeration are exactly the runtime cases the former multiple-provider check caught, and rejecting only a top-priority tie still allows the order-100 authz fallback to coexist.

authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/AuthzClient.java:95 — P1, confidence 100: `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader());` mutates a process-global first-write-wins singleton before `new AuthzClient(configuration)` performs remote discovery, so it works today, breaks when a first client construction fails or runs from a loader that sees only the order-100 fallback before a full provider becomes visible: the failed call leaves `cryptoProvider` permanently pinned and later `init` calls skip discovery, causing unrelated later crypto operations to hit the fallback's `UnsupportedOperationException`; the strongest rebuttal is that order-200 providers win when co-visible, but priority is never reconsidered after this first initialization and a failed constructor does not roll the singleton back.

authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:75 — P2, confidence 100: `throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported yet.");` is the advertised behavior for 17 methods on a provider registered in the process-global `CryptoIntegration`, so it works today, breaks when any shared/common call path needs a capability beyond the two ECDSA conversions and keystore creation: the request fails synchronously at runtime with an unchecked exception and there is no capability negotiation or fallback to another provider; the strongest rebuttal is that the authz client currently needs only ECDSA conversion, but global SPI registration exposes this object to every `CryptoIntegration.getProvider()` consumer and the singleton cannot swap providers after selection.

authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:63 — P2, confidence 100: `return KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider();` works today, breaks when any authz or shared dependency calls `getBouncyCastleProvider()`: the method silently returns the JVM default keystore provider (commonly `SUN`) rather than Bouncy Castle, so subsequent provider-specific algorithm lookup or casting fails far from initialization with misleading diagnostics; the strongest rebuttal is that this method is not used by the current ECDSA conversion path, but the provider implements and globally publishes the contract without marking the capability unsupported, turning a future call into silent wrong-provider propagation rather than an immediate explicit failure.

common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoProvider.java:44 — P1, confidence 100: the new abstract SPI method `int order();` expands “Add AuthzClientCryptoProvider” into a breaking requirement for every external `CryptoProvider`; when `CryptoIntegration` discovers an implementation compiled against the prior interface, its comparator invokes this missing method and throws `AbstractMethodError`, so an otherwise compatible deployment can no longer initialize crypto. The strongest counterargument is that every provider must declare precedence for coexistence with the authz provider, but a default `order()` or authz-specific fallback supplies that precedence without imposing an unrequested source/binary compatibility break on third-party providers.

common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — P1, confidence 100: `.sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed())` together with `return foundProviders.get(0);` at line 71 changes global multi-provider handling far beyond allowing the low-priority authz provider to coexist: when two full providers with the same new priority `200` (for example default and FIPS) are visible, initialization now silently selects whichever `ServiceLoader` encounters first instead of rejecting the ambiguity, so the process can run with the unintended cryptographic mode. The strongest counterargument is that ordering is necessary once authz-client adds a second provider, but retaining the ambiguity error whenever the highest priorities tie would satisfy that requirement while preserving the prior safety behavior for all non-authz provider combinations.

common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — severity=P2, confidence=75: verbatim vulnerable code `.sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed())` plus `return foundProviders.get(0);` (line 71) silently resolves equal-priority production crypto providers; trigger: `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider`, or `FIPS1402Provider` coexist and each returns `200`; failure: ServiceLoader enumeration order selects the active provider, so a FIPS-intended runtime that enumerates `DefaultCryptoProvider` first runs non-FIPS signing, encryption, and certificate operations instead of rejecting the ambiguous configuration; consequence: the deployment loses its configured cryptographic assurance and compliance boundary without a startup failure; strongest counterargument: normal packaging intends these providers to be mutually exclusive, but the new multi-provider branch expressly accepts coexistence and equal ranks provide no fail-closed protection against accidental/transitive classpath overlap.

authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:56 — P1 blocking, confidence 100: the sole oracle `Assert.assertArrayEquals(rsConcat, rsConcat2);` is a mirror assertion that asks the new decoder to accept output from the new encoder, so changing the encoder's sequence tag from constructed `0x30` to primitive `0x10` still passes because `ASN1Decoder.readTagNumber` masks the tag to `tag & 0x1f`, while an independent JCA `Signature.verify` rejects that non-DER signature; the trigger is any encoder defect shared or tolerated by the decoder, and the failure is shipped signatures that cannot be consumed outside this implementation. The strongest rebuttal is that `sign` originates from JCA, but that independently validates only the first DER-to-RS conversion—`asn1Des` is never returned to JCA—so the test must verify the reconstructed DER with the public key.

authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:47 — P1 blocking, confidence 100: `AuthzClientCryptoProvider prov = new AuthzClientCryptoProvider();` bypasses every changed integration behavior—the service descriptor, `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())`, and descending `CryptoProvider::order` selection—so a missing service entry, reversed comparator, or multi-provider regression leaves all three tests green while real `AuthzClient.create` either fails discovery or pins the process to the incomplete order-100 provider and later throws `UnsupportedOperationException`; the direct-construction test proves only helper logic, not the feature's runtime lifecycle. The strongest rebuttal is that provider discovery belongs to common infrastructure, but this change alters that infrastructure specifically to make the new authz service coexist, so an isolated-classloader test for authz-only discovery and a mixed-provider test asserting the order-200 winner are required.

authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:42 — P2 advisory, confidence 100: the fragile shared setup `keyPair = KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair();` leaves the curve provider-default and reuses that one key for ES256, ES384, and ES512, so the latter cases still carry P-256-sized `r`/`s` values; the trigger is the next edit to 48-/66-byte component handling or `ASN1Encoder.writeLength` for a P-521 sequence over 127 bytes, and the failure remains untested until actual ES384/ES512 traffic breaks. The strongest rebuttal is that `algorithm.getSignatureLength()` pads the round trip to each nominal width, but converting those padded arrays back through `BigInteger` strips the zeros before DER encoding, so the test never exercises native P-384/P-521 integers or the long-form length branch; initialize a curve-matched key per case and use stable vectors.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that when multiple providers have the same order (e.g., DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return 200), the selection becomes non-deterministic based on ServiceLoader encounter order. The diff shows the change from fail-fast (throwing exception when multiple providers found) to silently selecting the first after sorting. While this is intentional to allow the authz fallback (order 100) to coexist with full providers (order 200), the finding raises a valid architectural concern: ties among full providers are now silently resolved by encounter order rather than failing. This is a legitimate design/architecture concern about the change, not a bug per se since the behavior appears intentional, but it's a valid review point about potential non-determinism.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the test creates a single EC key pair using the default curve (likely P-256) and reuses it for all three algorithm tests (ES256, ES384, ES512). Looking at the diff, the test class creates one keyPair in the constructor and uses it across testES256(), testES384(), and testES512(). Each ECDSAAlgorithm has different signature lengths (ES256=64, ES384=96, ES512=132 based on typical ECDSA specs), but the same key is used for all. This means the ASN.1 encoding/decoding for the larger curves' boundary conditions isn't properly tested since the actual signature bytes won't match the expected lengths for ES384 and ES512. This is a legitimate test coverage gap for newly added crypto functionality.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:56 — P1 blocking, confidence 100: the sole oracle `Assert.assertArrayEquals(rsConcat, rsConcat2);` is a mirror assertion that asks the new decoder to accept output from the new encoder, so changing the encoder's sequence tag from constructed `0x30` to primitive `0x10` still passes because `ASN1Decoder.readTagNumber` masks the tag to `tag & 0x1f`, while an independent JCA `Signature.verify` rejects that non-DER signature; the trigger is any encoder defect shared or tolerated by the decoder, and the failure is shipped signatures that cannot be consumed outside this implementation. The strongest rebuttal is that `sign` originates from JCA, but that independently validates only the first DER-to-RS conversion—`asn1Des` is never returned to JCA—so the test must verify the reconstructed DER with the public key.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a test quality issue. Looking at the test in ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java, the test flow is: 1) JCA creates signature `sign`, 2) `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` converts to `rsConcat`, 3) `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` converts back to `asn1Des`, 4) `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` converts again to `rsConcat2`, 5) Assert `rsConcat == rsConcat2`. The finding is correct that this is a 'mirror assertion' - it only verifies round-trip consistency between the encoder and decoder, not that the encoded DER is actually valid. If both encoder and decoder had a shared bug (e.g., wrong tag), the test would still pass. The test never verifies `asn1Des` against JCA's Signature.verify(). This is a legitimate test coverage gap for newly added crypto code, though it's not a bug in the implementation itself - it's a missing test case.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a test quality issue in the new test file. The test uses a single EC key pair generated with default curve (P-256) but tests ES256, ES384, and ES512 algorithms. Looking at the test code, `keyPair = KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` creates one key, and the same key is used for all three algorithm tests. While the test does exercise the ASN1Encoder/Decoder round-trip, it doesn't actually test with proper P-384 or P-521 keys. The finding's technical analysis about padding and BigInteger stripping zeros is valid - the test won't exercise the full range of integer sizes that would occur with actual P-384/P-521 keys. This is a legitimate test coverage concern for newly added crypto code, not a bug in production code, but an important gap in test coverage.
